listeningParts.title: Enrolling on a dressmaking course
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man phones a community college to enrol on an evening course in dressmaking.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, Brookfield Community College, Siobhan speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hi there. I'm calling about the evening classes in dressmaking. I saw a leaflet about them, and I'd like to find out a bit more before I sign up.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Of course. We actually have two dressmaking courses starting this autumn: Introduction to Dressmaking, which is for complete beginners, and Dressmaking Two, for people who already know the basics. Have you done any sewing before?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Only very simple things, like sewing on buttons. I've never used a sewing machine.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Then the introduction course is definitely the right one. It runs on two evenings, but the Thursday group is already full, I'm afraid. There are still a few places on Tuesdays, from seven until half past nine.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Tuesday would actually suit me better anyway. When does it start?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The first class is on the twenty-third of September, and it runs for ten weeks, with a break for one week in the middle of October, when the college is closed.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: A break in October? I hadn't realised the college closed then.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, it's the mid-term holiday for the schools that share the site, so the whole campus shuts for a week. The course still has ten full sessions, though; the final class just finishes a week later, at the beginning of December. Each class is two and a half hours long, with a short tea break halfway through.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. Okay. And what does it cost?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The standard fee is one hundred and eighty-five pounds. If you're a student, over sixty-five or receiving certain benefits, there's a reduced fee of one hundred and fifty pounds, but you'd need to show proof of that when you enrol.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: No, I'll be paying the standard fee. Does that include materials?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: It includes the use of the sewing machines, the patterns and thread, but you'll need to buy your own fabric. In the first few weeks, you'll learn how to use the machine safely, how to take measurements and how to read a pattern. Your first project is a simple apron, and by the end of the course most people have made a skirt or a pair of loose trousers that fits them properly.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds great. Is there anything I need to bring to the first class?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: The tutor asks everyone to bring a good pair of scissors, the kind that are only used for cutting fabric, because ordinary ones aren't sharp enough and they damage the cloth. And a notebook is useful, too. You don't need fabric for the first week.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Where's the best place to buy fabric? I'm new to the area.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Most of our students go to a shop called Thread and Bobbin, on Mill Street, near the bus station. They give a ten per cent discount if you show your college card.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Thanks. And where exactly are the classes held?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: In the Harland Building, which is the new building behind the main car park. It's room fourteen, on the ground floor. There's a lift, but you won't need it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Okay. Can I enrol over the phone?

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Yes, I can take your details now, and then you can pay online. Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Whitcombe. That's W-H-I-T-C-O-M-B-E.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Thank you. And a contact phone number?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Yes, it's oh seven seven one two, four eight three, five six oh.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: Lovely. And just for our records, how did you hear about the course? You mentioned a leaflet.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's right. Actually, my neighbour gave it to me. She did the course last year and loved it, so she recommended it to me.

dialogue.speaker: Receptionist
dialogue.text: That's good to hear. I'll put down a personal recommendation, then. One last thing: if you need to miss a class, please let the tutor know in advance, because she'll sometimes give you some practice to do at home so you don't fall behind.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Will do. Thanks very much for your help.

listeningParts.title: A sustainable fashion festival
listeningParts.contextDescription: An organiser talks on local radio about a week-long festival on repairing and reusing clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And now, joining me in the studio is Kirsty Doyle, who's organising next month's Wear It Again festival. Kirsty, welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Thanks for having me. Wear It Again is a week of events about making our clothes last longer, through repairing them, swapping them and redesigning them. It's the third year we've held it, and it's grown a lot. In the first year we had about four hundred visitors, and last year we had nearly two thousand.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: Why do you think it's become so popular?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: I think people are increasingly uncomfortable about how many clothes are thrown away. But honestly, the main reason people tell us they come is the cost. Prices have gone up so much that learning to repair a favourite jacket, instead of replacing it, makes a real difference to their budget. The environmental side often comes second.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: So what's on the programme this year?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: The week opens on Monday with the Repair Café in the town library. Volunteers with sewing skills will be there all day to help you fix things like broken zips, torn pockets and holes in jumpers. It's not a service where you leave your clothes and pick them up later, though. The idea is that the volunteers show you how to do the repair yourself, so that next time you won't need them.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: On Tuesday evening, we have a talk at the arts centre by a textile historian, about how people looked after their clothes in the past, when clothing was so expensive that a coat might be passed down through several generations. That's free, but places are limited, so you'll need to reserve a seat on our website.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Wednesday is our clothes swap, which is always the busiest event. It's very simple: you bring up to five items of clothing that are clean and in good condition, and you receive a token for each one, which you can exchange for something someone else has brought. Anything that's left at the end goes to a local charity.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: On Thursday there's an upcycling workshop for teenagers, run by students from the college's fashion department. Upcycling means turning old clothes into something new and better, so for example cutting up old jeans to make a bag. That workshop's for thirteen to eighteen-year-olds only, and there's a small charge of five pounds to cover the materials.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: Then on Friday we're trying something new: a session with a professional tailor, who'll explain what kinds of alterations are worth paying for and which aren't. For example, shortening trousers or taking in a waist is usually straightforward, but changing the shoulders of a jacket is very difficult and often costs more than the jacket itself.

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: And we finish on Saturday with a fashion show in the town square, where all the outfits are second-hand or made from old clothes. Children are very welcome at that, and there'll be face painting and music as well.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: It sounds like a full week. Is there anything people should do to prepare?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: For the Repair Café, please bring your own thread if you can, in a colour that matches the item, because we can't possibly have every colour. And for the swap, please wash everything before you bring it. We do check, and we have to turn away a surprising number of things every year.

dialogue.speaker: Presenter
dialogue.text: And if people want to get involved as volunteers?

dialogue.speaker: Kirsty
dialogue.text: We'd love that. We especially need people on Wednesday to help sort the clothes into sizes before the doors open. You don't need any special skills for that, just a bit of patience. There's a form on the website, or you can come to our planning meeting next Thursday at the library.

listeningParts.title: Designing a sustainable school uniform
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two design students, Priya and Tom, discuss their project with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, Priya, Tom, your project is to redesign the uniform for a local secondary school so that it's more sustainable. Where have you got to?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We've finished the research stage. We started by surveying parents at the school, and we had nearly three hundred replies, which was far more than we expected.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Excellent. What did they say?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: The thing that came up again and again was durability. Parents said that the school jumpers, in particular, wear out at the elbows within a few months, and that the trousers lose their colour after being washed a lot. Price was mentioned too, of course, but less often than we'd assumed.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: And quite a few parents complained that the uniform can only be bought from one shop, which is expensive. That's not really a design issue, but we've mentioned it in our report.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. Now, what about materials? That's the heart of the project.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: We compared four main fibres. The current uniform is mostly a polyester and cotton blend. Polyester is cheap and very hard-wearing, and it dries quickly, which parents like. But it's made from oil, and every time it's washed, it releases tiny plastic fibres that end up in rivers and the sea.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: The other problem with blends is recycling. Because the two fibres are mixed together in the same thread, it's very difficult to separate them at the end of the garment's life, so most blended clothing can't be recycled into new fabric.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's an important point, and one that a lot of people miss. What about cotton on its own?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Cotton is comfortable and breathable, but conventional cotton needs a great deal of water and often a lot of pesticides. Organic cotton avoids the pesticides, but it's more expensive, and on its own it's not as hard-wearing as a blend.

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We were quite interested in wool for the jumpers. It's naturally resistant to smells, so it doesn't need washing as often, and it lasts a long time if it's looked after. The disadvantage is that it can shrink if it's washed at the wrong temperature, and some children find it itchy.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: And the fourth?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: Lyocell, which is made from wood pulp. The chemicals used to dissolve the wood are recovered and reused in what's called a closed-loop process, so it has a much lower impact than most other fibres made from wood. It's soft and strong, but we couldn't find much information on how well it survives years of school use.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So what have you decided?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: For the shirts, organic cotton. For the trousers and skirts, we're suggesting a fabric made from recycled polyester, because durability matters most there, and at least that reuses plastic that already exists. And for the jumpers, wool, with patches on the elbows built into the design from the start.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I like the idea of the elbow patches. It turns a weakness into a feature. But I'd question the recycled polyester. It still sheds microfibres, doesn't it?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: It does. We've suggested that the school could give families a special washing bag that catches the fibres, but we know it isn't a perfect solution.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then say that clearly in your evaluation. Examiners respect honesty about limitations. What's the next step?

dialogue.speaker: Priya
dialogue.text: We're making prototypes. We'd like to test them by asking a few pupils to wear them for a month, but we're not sure whether that's allowed.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: You'll need permission from the school, and from the parents, as the pupils are under eighteen. Speak to the head teacher first. In the meantime, you could test the fabrics in the lab here; we have a machine that rubs fabric repeatedly to measure how quickly it wears.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.text: That would be really useful. Thanks.

listeningParts.title: The invention of synthetic fibres
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a design history course on how artificial and synthetic fibres were developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning. Last week we looked at the natural fibres that people have used for thousands of years: cotton, linen, wool and silk. Today we're going to look at what happened when chemists began to make fibres in the laboratory, a development that has completely transformed the clothes we wear. Today, in fact, synthetic fibres account for considerably more than half of all the fibre produced in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The story begins with silk. For centuries, silk was the most desirable fabric in Europe, but it was extremely expensive, and in the nineteenth century European silk production was badly damaged by diseases affecting silkworms. Several inventors therefore tried to create an artificial silk. The first to succeed commercially was a French aristocrat, Count Hilaire de Chardonnet, who made fibres from cellulose, the substance that forms the walls of plant cells. He displayed his fabric at the Paris Exhibition of 1889, where it attracted a great deal of attention. Unfortunately, the chemical process he used made the material dangerously flammable, and it was some time before safer methods were developed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One of these safer methods was the viscose process, patented in 1892 by three British chemists. In this process, cellulose, usually from wood pulp, is dissolved and then forced through tiny holes to form threads. The fibre it produced became known in the 1920s as rayon, and it was widely used for dresses, linings and underwear. It's important to understand that rayon isn't fully synthetic. It's sometimes called semi-synthetic, because it's made from a natural material that has been chemically processed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The first truly synthetic fibre, made entirely from chemicals, came from the American company DuPont. In the late 1920s, DuPont hired a young chemist named Wallace Carothers to carry out basic research into polymers, which are very long chain-like molecules. In 1935, his team produced a polymer that could be drawn out into strong, elastic threads. This was nylon. Interestingly, the first product made from it was not clothing at all, but toothbrush bristles, which went on sale in 1938.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Nylon's great success, however, came with women's stockings. Until then, stockings had been made of silk, which was expensive and ran easily. When nylon stockings went on sale across the United States in 1940, they sold out almost immediately. But soon after the United States entered the Second World War, nylon production was redirected to military uses, especially parachutes, which had previously been made of silk, as well as ropes and tents. Nylon stockings became so scarce that some women drew a line down the back of their legs to imitate the seam.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Meanwhile, in Britain, two chemists working for a textile company in Manchester, John Whinfield and James Dickson, developed polyester in 1941. Polyester became enormously popular after the war, because it's strong, cheap and resistant to creasing, which meant clothes didn't need ironing. Today it's by far the most widely used fibre in the world. A further important development came in 1958, when another DuPont chemist, Joseph Shivers, invented elastane, a fibre that can stretch to several times its own length and then return to its original shape. It's better known by its brand name, Lycra, and it made possible the close-fitting sportswear that we now take for granted.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: These fibres brought enormous benefits. Clothing became cheaper, easier to care for and more varied than ever before. But they also brought problems that their inventors couldn't have foreseen. Most synthetic fibres are made from oil, and they don't break down naturally, so discarded clothes can remain in landfill for centuries. And researchers have found that synthetic garments shed tiny fibres every time they're washed, which pass through water treatment plants and end up in rivers and oceans. Next week, we'll look at some of the new materials that designers are developing in response.

readingPassages.title: The story of indigo
paragraphs: Of all the colours that people have used to dye cloth, few have such a long and dramatic history as indigo, the deep blue now most familiar from the denim of jeans. The dye has been used on every inhabited continent, and its trade has made fortunes, caused rebellions and helped to launch the modern chemical industry. Remarkably, the blue of a pair of jeans bought today is chemically identical to the blue that was being produced thousands of years ago, although the way it is made has changed completely.

Indigo can be obtained from a number of different plants, but the most important has been Indigofera tinctoria, a shrub that grows in tropical regions and was cultivated especially in India, from which the dye takes its name. In Europe, a similar blue was obtained from woad, a plant of the cabbage family that grows well in cooler climates, though it contains much less of the colouring substance. The oldest known indigo-dyed fabric, however, comes from neither region: in 2016, researchers reported that fragments of cotton cloth found at Huaca Prieta in Peru had been dyed with indigo around six thousand years ago.

Indigo is unlike most natural dyes, because the colouring substance cannot simply be extracted by boiling the plant in water. The leaves do not even look blue. Instead, they are soaked and allowed to ferment, a process that releases a colourless compound which reacts with oxygen to form solid indigo. This is then dried into cakes for transport. Because indigo does not dissolve in water, the dyer must convert it back into a soluble form in a vat. Cloth dipped into this liquid comes out yellowish-green, and only turns blue as it is exposed to the air. Darker shades are produced by dipping the cloth many times.

When Portuguese and Dutch merchants began importing large quantities of Indian indigo into Europe by sea in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the woad growers of France and Germany, whose industry had made some regions extremely wealthy, faced ruin. They campaigned against the foreign dye, claiming that it was harmful and that it damaged cloth, and several governments introduced laws to restrict or even ban its use. In the end, however, indigo was simply too good to resist. It produced stronger colours more cheaply, and by the end of the seventeenth century the woad industry had largely collapsed.

European powers soon began producing indigo in their colonies. In the 1740s, a young woman named Eliza Lucas, who was managing her family's plantations in South Carolina, experimented with growing indigo, and within a few years it had become one of the colony's most valuable exports. This prosperity, however, depended on the labour of enslaved Africans. In India, British planters in Bengal forced local farmers to grow indigo instead of food crops, often on very unfair terms. In 1859, thousands of farmers refused to continue, in a protest that became known as the Indigo Revolt and that eventually led the authorities to investigate the planters' methods.

The end of the natural indigo trade came not from protest but from chemistry. In the nineteenth century, chemists in Europe, and especially in Germany, were learning how to manufacture dyes from substances found in coal tar. The German chemist Adolf von Baeyer succeeded in making indigo in the laboratory in 1880, and he worked out its chemical structure a few years later. Developing a process that was cheap enough for industrial use took much longer, but in 1897 the German company BASF began selling synthetic indigo. Within a few decades, natural indigo had almost disappeared from world markets, with disastrous consequences for growers in India.

Meanwhile, indigo had found a new use. In 1873, a tailor named Jacob Davis and a merchant named Levi Strauss received a patent in the United States for work trousers strengthened with metal rivets, and these were made from tough cotton cloth dyed with indigo. One feature of indigo explains the character of denim. The dye attaches mainly to the surface of the cotton threads rather than penetrating to their centre, so as jeans are worn and washed, the colour gradually rubs away, revealing the white core of the thread. The faded look that once showed long years of hard work later became highly fashionable.

Today, almost all indigo is synthetic and made from chemicals derived from oil. Producing it, and especially converting it into a soluble form for dyeing, involves chemicals that can pollute rivers if waste water is not properly treated, and some textile regions have suffered serious environmental damage as a result. Researchers are now exploring cleaner methods, including the use of bacteria to produce the dye, while a small number of farmers and craft dyers have returned to growing indigo plants. It seems that the long story of this ancient blue is still far from over.

readingPassages.title: The true cost of cheap clothes
paragraphs: For most of human history, clothes were valuable possessions. Fabric was spun and woven by hand, garments were repaired again and again, and good clothing was often left to relatives in wills. Even in the mid-twentieth century, many families in wealthy countries bought only a few new items each year. Today the situation is very different. It has been estimated that global clothing production roughly doubled in the first fifteen years of this century, while the average number of times a garment is worn before being thrown away fell considerably over the same period.

This change is largely the result of a business model known as fast fashion. Traditional fashion companies planned their collections many months in advance and released them in two main seasons each year. Fast-fashion retailers, by contrast, design, manufacture and deliver new styles in a matter of weeks, responding quickly to trends seen on catwalks, in celebrity photographs or, increasingly, on social media. Their shops receive new stock constantly, which encourages customers to visit often and to buy before a style disappears. Prices are kept low by producing in very large quantities in countries where wages are low.

The environmental costs of this model begin with raw materials. Cotton is one of the world's most water-intensive crops: one widely quoted estimate suggests that around 2,700 litres of water are needed to produce the cotton for a single T-shirt. Irrigation for cotton growing contributed to one of the worst environmental disasters of the twentieth century, the shrinking of the Aral Sea in Central Asia. Synthetic fibres, which now make up the majority of the fibre used in clothing, avoid this problem, but they are made from oil, and dyeing and finishing fabric of all kinds uses large amounts of energy and chemicals.

The problems continue long after clothes are sold. A report published in 2017 by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation calculated that the equivalent of one rubbish truck full of textiles is sent to landfill or burned every second, and that less than one per cent of the material used to make clothing is recycled into new clothing. Much of what is donated to charity in wealthy countries is exported, and some ends up in markets in countries such as Ghana, where traders say that a growing share of the bales they buy is of such poor quality that it cannot be sold and must be thrown away.

There are human costs as well. The low prices of fast fashion depend on low wages in countries such as Bangladesh, Cambodia and Vietnam, and working conditions in some factories are poor or dangerous. In April 2013, the Rana Plaza building near Dhaka in Bangladesh, which housed several garment factories, collapsed, killing more than eleven hundred people. Workers had been ordered to return to the building the day after cracks had appeared in its walls. The disaster led many international brands to sign an agreement to fund independent safety inspections of the factories that supplied them.

Faced with growing criticism, the fashion industry has begun to respond. Many companies now offer clothes made from organic cotton or recycled polyester, and some run schemes in which customers can return old clothes to shops. Critics argue, however, that such initiatives are small compared with the volume of new clothing being produced, and that recycling is of limited value while the technology for turning old garments back into fibre of good quality remains in its early stages. Some describe these efforts as 'greenwashing': presenting a business as more environmentally friendly than it really is.

Governments have also begun to act. In France, a law passed in 2020 made it illegal for companies to destroy unsold clothing and other non-food products, requiring them instead to donate or recycle them. Other proposals include making producers financially responsible for collecting and processing their products at the end of their life, and requiring labels that show the environmental impact of a garment. Such measures aim to change the behaviour of companies, but many experts believe that lasting change will also depend on consumers.

There are signs that attitudes are shifting. The market for second-hand clothing has grown rapidly, helped by websites and apps that make buying and selling used items easy, and clothing rental services have appeared for special occasions. Repair is also enjoying a revival. Nevertheless, the simplest solution may be the least fashionable one: buying fewer clothes of better quality and wearing them for longer. One study after another suggests that extending the life of a garment is among the most effective ways of reducing its environmental impact.

readingPassages.title: Should fashion designs be protected from copying?
paragraphs: Within days of a new collection appearing on the catwalk, cheaper versions of its most striking pieces often appear in high-street shops. To the designers concerned, this can feel like theft. A novelist whose book is copied, or a musician whose song is reproduced without permission, can usually take legal action. Yet in many countries, a designer whose dress is copied has surprisingly little protection. Whether that situation is unfair, or whether it is actually good for fashion, is a question that has divided lawyers, economists and designers themselves.

The legal position varies considerably from one country to another. In the United States, copyright law has traditionally treated clothing as a 'useful article', meaning that its practical function prevents it from being protected in the way that a painting or a sculpture would be. Brand names and logos can be registered as trademarks, and a small number of genuinely new technical features can be patented, but the overall shape and cut of a garment are generally free for anyone to copy. Several bills that would have created special protection for fashion designs were introduced in the US Congress from 2006 onwards, but none of them became law.

There has been one notable change. In 2017, in a case about cheerleading uniforms, the US Supreme Court ruled that decorative elements of a garment, in that case a pattern of stripes and chevrons, could be protected by copyright if they could be imagined as a work of art separately from the garment itself. The decision was welcomed by many designers, but legal experts disagree about how far it extends, and it does not protect the basic design of clothes.

Europe takes a different approach. Under European Union law, a design that is new and has individual character is automatically protected against copying for three years from the date it is first made public, without any need for registration. Designers who want longer protection can register their designs, which may then be protected for up to twenty-five years. Some European countries go further: France, for instance, has long allowed clothing designs to be protected in a similar way to works of art. Despite this, copying remains widespread in Europe too, partly because legal action is slow and expensive.

Perhaps surprisingly, some researchers argue that weak protection benefits the fashion industry. In an influential article published in 2006, the American law professors Kal Raustiala and Christopher Sprigman described what they called the 'piracy paradox'. They pointed out that the American fashion industry is highly creative and commercially successful despite, or perhaps because of, the freedom to copy. In their view, copying spreads new styles quickly, so that they soon become too common to be exclusive. Fashionable consumers then look for something new, and designers must keep innovating. Copying, in other words, speeds up the cycle of fashion.

Not everyone accepts this argument. Critics point out that it may describe the position of large, established fashion houses well, since they have famous brand names that protect their sales even when their designs are copied. Independent designers are in a much weaker position. A young designer who produces an original garment may see a copy on sale at a fraction of the price before she has had a chance to sell her own, and she is unlikely to have the money to fight a legal battle against a large retailer. For such designers, copying can mean the difference between building a business and abandoning it.

In my view, the critics have the stronger case, although the piracy paradox contains an important truth. Fashion has always depended on borrowing and imitation, and a law that allowed designers to claim ownership of every new sleeve or neckline would be both unworkable and harmful to creativity. But there is a significant difference between being inspired by a trend and producing an almost exact copy of a particular garment within weeks. The current system in countries such as the United States effectively rewards the companies that are best at copying, rather than those that are best at designing.

The European model, which offers short but automatic protection, seems to me a reasonable compromise. Three years is long enough for a designer to benefit from an original idea, but short enough not to prevent the natural spread of styles. What is needed, I believe, is not stronger laws so much as cheaper and quicker ways of enforcing them, so that the protection that exists on paper is available to small designers as well as large ones. Without that, the debate about copying will continue to be decided by those who can afford the best lawyers.

writingTask1.title: Making fabric from plastic bottles
writingTask1.instructions: The diagram below shows how used plastic bottles are recycled to make polyester fabric for clothing. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
processSteps: Used plastic bottles are collected from recycling bins
Bottles are sorted by colour and labels and caps are removed
Bottles are washed and shredded into small flakes
Flakes are melted and formed into small pellets
Pellets are melted again and pushed through tiny holes to form fibres
Fibres are stretched, cooled and spun into yarn
Yarn is woven or knitted into polyester fabric
Fabric is dyed and cut to make clothing
keyOverviewPoints: The process has eight stages, beginning with the collection of used bottles and ending with finished clothing.
The plastic is melted twice, first to make pellets and then to produce fibres that are spun into yarn.
